analysis.one_liner: Creates a commission to recommend repeal of federal regulations more than ten years old.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to build an up-or-down repeal process for old federal regulations was referred to two House committees and died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 978, the Regulatory Improvement Act of 2017, would have created a commission — modeled loosely on the military base-closing commissions — to go through federal regulations finalized at least ten years earlier, pick a list of rules to repeal or replace, and force Congress to vote up or down on that package with no amendments allowed. The bill was introduced by Rep. Kyrsten Sinema, a Democrat, with nine cosponsors [S4]. It was referred to two House committees, Oversight and Government Reform and Rules [S5], and no further action was ever taken; the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1]. Nothing about the regulations on the books changed as a result.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be businesses and other regulated parties — from banks to manufacturers to polluters — whose oldest regulatory obligations would be systematically reviewed for repeal, with a closed up-or-down vote making it politically easy for members to clear a large deregulation package at once. Industry groups had long sought exactly this kind of mechanism, because individual repeal votes force members to defend cutting specific protections, while a bundled package lets all cuts pass with a single yes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a commission of experts in government service, regulatory policy, and economics to review federal regulations that were finalized at least ten years before and recommend a package of repeals or cheaper alternatives [S3].
Congress would then vote on the commission's package as a single up-or-down bill, with no amendments allowed in either chamber, making it easier to enact a large set of repeals at once [S3].
The commission would be exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act, the law that normally requires federal advisory bodies to meet in public with balanced membership and open records [S3].

The bill states its purpose includes reducing regulatory costs 'while protecting public health and safety,' reflecting the sponsors' framing that outdated rules are a burden without public benefit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost, if it had passed, would fall on the people who rely on regulations that a ten-year cutoff sweeps in. Many of the most important federal protections — workplace safety standards, environmental limits, financial rules, consumer safeguards — are decades old and would have been candidates for repeal, with the bill's closed vote giving defenders no chance to remove a bad repeal from the package. The public would also lose the transparency guarantees of the Federal Advisory Committee Act for the commission's work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, workers, and the public relying on old protections

drawbacks.text: A blanket ten-year cutoff would put long-standing protections on the repeal chopping block: many health, safety, and financial rules are older than ten years not because they are obsolete but because the problems they address persist [S3].

The commission would be exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act, so its meetings, membership balance, and records would not be subject to the transparency rules that normally apply to federal advisory bodies [S3].

The up-or-down, no-amendments vote structure means members of Congress could not strike even one bad repeal from the package, forcing a single all-or-nothing decision on every rule the commission targets [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real idea here: federal rules do accumulate cruft, and a systematic review could retire genuinely outdated requirements that burden small businesses. But the design stacks the deck in favor of repeal — a ten-year automatic cutoff, a commission exempt from open-meeting and balanced-membership rules, and a closed vote that bars any amendment. The bill's stated goal of protecting public health and safety sits uneasily with a process that would subject old clean-air, workplace-safety, and consumer rules to a bundled repeal vote with no opportunity to defend them individually.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kyrsten Sinema introduced the bill in the House on February 7, 2017 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and to the Committee on Rules on February 7, 2017 [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history; it was never reported out of committee or considered on the floor [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one moved ahead, and no one lost ground: the bill died in committee, so the existing rules on the books — including the older health, safety, environmental, and financial regulations the commission would have targeted — remained in force unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill died untouched in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and never reached a vote, so no party split can be measured; regulatory-reduction commissions of this kind typically draw business-oriented support from both parties, and its nine cosponsors cut across affiliations [S4].

industries.industry: Regulated industries (finance, manufacturing, energy, and other business sectors)
industries.note: If enacted, a standing commission to repeal regulations older than ten years would systematically reduce compliance costs across every regulated sector, with a bundled up-or-down vote that removes the political cost of cutting any single protection.
Agencies would lose work hours and established rules to the commission's review, but they would also gain a vehicle for retiring genuinely obsolete rules they lack the resources to revisit.
